claims.text: At stage-3 DonHang.Api's connection string names Database=donhang, while DonHang.Notifications uses Database=donhang_notifications; at stage-2 QueuedNotifier staged a pending notifications row in the order's DbContext.
A message broker accepts messages from one program and keeps them in a queue until another program takes them, so the sender needs the broker, not the receiver, to be running.

claims.text: Each order message is a JSON body holding the order id, the customer's email and name and when the change happened (OrderMessage: OrderId, CustomerEmail, CustomerName, OccurredAt).
notifications.order-events is the queue the Notifications service reads: RabbitMqTopology declares it and OrderEventsConsumer, a hosted service, consumes it.

With notifications stopped, POST /api/v1/orders answers 201 and 1 message waits in notifications.order-events with 0 email jobs; after the service starts again, 0 messages wait and the order's email job is sent.

The API process (OutboxRelay, registered in DonHang.Api/Program.cs:48) sends the message to RabbitMQ shortly after the order is saved, not during the request; the lesson defers how to backend.l3.outbox-pattern.

In Notifications, OrderEventsConsumer turns each message into a pending notifications row and NotificationSender sends those rows as emails to Mailpit (Smtp__Host mailpit), as it did inside the api until stage-2.
Calling Notifications over HTTP while placing an order would make the order wait when Notifications is slow, and force failing the order or giving up the email when it is down.

claims.text: With a broker between them, neither the API nor Notifications needs the other running at the same moment; each only talks to RabbitMQ.

claims.text: NotifyCustomerOnOrderEvents loads the customer and puts customer.Email and customer.FullName into every OrderMessage it adds; the customers table lives in the donhang database.

A call needs the other side to answer now, a message only needs the broker to accept it; opposing view: when the caller needs an answer before it can respond, a direct call is the right tool, since a one-way message brings no answer back.
Reading another service's table would tie the two services together again; if they are to stay apart, a missing field is added to the message instead.

notifications-down.sh stops notifications, places an order as customer 1, counts the messages in notifications.order-events, starts the service again and waits for the email job; a trap restarts the service on exit.
